title: Avoid delete-and-insert for non-indexed UPDATE RETURNING
body:
Closes https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb/issues/25654

In the current implementation, [`LogicalUpdate::columns`](https://github.com/dentiny/duckdb/blob/ca5ce12b7dd33555f58d81ade0990442cb6eefca/src/include/duckdb/planner/operator/logical_update.hpp#L38) represents both columns explicitly modified by SET and columns merely materialized for constraint checks or RETURNING.

For `UPDATE ... RETURNING`, [BindUpdateConstraints](https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb/blob/88902aaa3972216c928c8e79a89217a413be414c/src/catalog/catalog_entry/table_catalog_entry.cpp#L297-L302) materialized every physical column through `BindExtraColumns`. Those columns were appended to `update.columns`, which was subsequently used to check constraints.

As a result, RETURNING made an update to a non-key column appear to modify the primary key, incorrectly rewriting it as DELETE + INSERT. Deleting the referenced parent row then produced a false foreign key violation.

In this PR, I split the responsibility into two parts:
- `referenced_columns`, which represents columns materialized for constraints, RETURNING, or reinsertion
- `columns_to_update`: columns explicitly targeted by the SET clause

title: Skip parse/plan/optimize for Connection::BeginTransaction/Commit/Rollback
body: Hi team, I'm playing with WAL replay and found for small transactions (i.e., BEGIN; single row append; COMMIT;) replay latency is linear in the number of transactions Example benchmark ```py for n in (10000, 50000, 200000): with open(f'/tmp/wal_bench/A{n}.sql', 'w') as f: f.write("CREATE TABLE t(a INT, b VARCHAR);\n") for i in range(n): f.write(f"BEGIN; INSERT INTO t VALUES ({i}, 'row_{i}'); COMMIT;\n") ``` Checkpoint on shutdown is disabled, WAL auto checkpoint is set to an unreachably high value to guarantee replay takes all the insertions and transactions. I did a flamegraph on WAL replay, from the rendered graph, we could easily tell most of the time is spent on `BeginTransaction` and `Commit`, with planner + optimizer + executor work inside, which is not necessary for WAL replay. The actual replay work takes only ~10% of the CPU time. The commit pseudocode looks like (asked opus-4.7 to draw the callstack), begin transaction looks alike ```sh con.Commit() ← what we call └─ Query("COMMIT") ← Connection::Commit implementation └─ Parser::ParseQuery("COMMIT") └─ Binder::Bind └─ Planner::CreatePlan └─ Optimizer::Optimizer(binder, context) ← every rewrite rule is constructed! (ContainsToInClauseRule, EnumCompareSimplification, MoveConstantsRule, StringPrefixRule, ...) └─ PhysicalPlanGenerator::CreatePlan └─ Executor::ExecuteTask └─ PhysicalTransaction::GetDataInternal(COMMIT) └─ switch(type): case COMMIT: if (IsAutoCommit()) throw ... client.transaction.Commit(); ← the one line that does real work client.SuppressInterrupts(); ``` So in this PR, I propose to simplify the replay to skip all the redundant work and only include necessary work - Start a transaction with `TransactionContext::SetAutoCommit(false)` - Commit a transaction with `TransactionContext::Commit` Performance comparison before and after the change | Scenario | Before | After | Speedup | |---------------------------------|---------:|----------:|-----------:| | 10 k single-row transactions | 0.72 s | **0.11 s**| **6.5×** | | 50 k single-row transactions | 3.65 s | **0.59 s**| **6.2×** | | 200 k single-row transactions | 14.16 s | **2.04 s**| **6.9×** | | 2000 CREATE/INSERT/DROP cycles | 0.48 s | **0.06 s**| **8.0×** | | 5 M-row single INSERT | 0.02 s | 0.02 s | no change | | 200 k rows + 10× UPDATE-all | 0.05 s | 0.05 s | no change |

title: [async results] Add a unified QueryResult type
body:
Stack (only land in order):
- [x] #25287 Adds a drain mode to the benchmark runner to distinguish between materializing and dropping chunks, and two regression tests
- [x] #25288 Enable the two new regression tests
- [x] #25257 Result buffer redesign
- [ ] This PR
- [ ] Allow setting a notifier callback when submitting a query. The callback will be called when data is available or when a query errors, finishes or is interrupted.
- [ ] Deprecate the "custom collector" idea with an output format API that uses a format agnostic (but managed) buffer underneath. Move the Arrow collector to this API as the first consumer.
- [ ] Expose async query execution in the C API v2

This PR reworks the result type, and introduces async query execution. It:
- Adds / adapts blocking and non-blocking query execution methods on `ClientContext`.
- Replaces the existing result types with a single `QueryResult`.
- Adds a `QueryResultStream` that can take ownership of a `QueryResult` and provides streaming semantics.
- Adds polling and non-blocking fetch methods.

### Blocking and Non-blocking Query Execution

`PendingQueryResult`, `MaterializedQueryResult`, and `StreamQueryResult` are replaced with a single, unified `QueryResult` type. You get a `QueryResult` by running a query, either through a family of non-blocking methods (`Submit`) or a family of blocking methods (`Query`):
- `ClientContext::Submit`: (non-blocking) submit a query or statement. The engine runs it iff `threads - external_threads > 0`, but produces no data until the caller either calls a materializing method on the result, or moves the result into a `QueryResultStream` (see below).
- `ClientContext::Query`: (blocking) runs a query or statement to completion, and returns the result containing all data materialized.

### `QueryResult`

A `QueryResult` provides:
- `QueryResultState Poll()`: (non-materializing) Returns the result's current state
- `QueryResultState ExecuteTask()`: (non-materializing) Executes a single task, not exactly like but comparable to `PendingQueryResult::ExecuteTask()`. It drives execution of the pipeline, but it will not settle the result buffer on its own. The caller must at some point either call e.g. `Materialize()` or move the result into a `QueryResultStream` and continue calling `ExecuteTask` and `TryFetch` on that.
- `void Materialize()`: (materializing, non-blocking) Lets the engine materialize the data. Note that if the engine does not have any threads of its own, the caller must still call one of the blocking methods below and participate in task execution.
- `void Complete()`: (materializing, blocking) Like `Materialize()`, but will block (and participate in execution) until execution is finished.
- `ColumnDataCollection &Collection()`: (materializing, blocking) Like `Complete()`, but will return a reference to the resulting CDC.
- `unique_ptr<ColumnDataCollection> TakeCollection()`: (materializing, blocking) Like `Collection()` but will pass ownership of the CDC to the caller.
- `unique_ptr<DataChunk> Fetch()`: (materializing, blocking) Fetches the next chunk. Will participate in execution.
- `unique_ptr<DataChunk> FetchRaw()`: (materializing, blocking) Like `Fetch()`, but will not normalize vector types.

### `QueryResultStream`

A `QueryResultStream` provides streaming semantics. It can be created by giving it ownership of a `QueryResult` that does not have materialized data yet (i.e. whose result sink buffer has not been decided yet).

The reason to introduce it, is that cdc-backed results do behave differently than buffer-backed results, because the latter is read-once while the former is not. For example, you _could_ support Materialize and TakeCollection on a stream, but they would be significantly slower since these operations would go through the streaming buffer. And Materializing a stream after reading one or two chunks is not the same as reading a few chunks from a CDC-backed buffer and then asking for the CDC.

Once created, a stream provides:
- `QueryResultState Poll()`: Returns the result's current state
- `QueryResultState ExecuteTask()`: Like `QueryResult::ExecuteTask()`. Can be used together with `TryFetch` to stream chunks out in a single-threaded application.
- `QueryResultState TryFetch(unique_ptr<DataChunk> &out_chunk)`: (non-blocking) Like `Poll()` but fetches a chunk if it's available.
- `unique_ptr<DataChunk> Fetch()`:  (blocking) Fetches the next chunk. Will participate in execution.

title: Make EXPORT DATABASE round-trip quoted empty strings and null strings
body:
Fixes #25501.

`EXPORT DATABASE` followed by `IMPORT DATABASE` with the default CSV format reads every empty string back as `NULL`:

```sql
CREATE TABLE t(v VARCHAR);
INSERT INTO t VALUES (NULL), (''), ('NULL');
EXPORT DATABASE 'out';
-- fresh database
IMPORT DATABASE 'out';
SELECT count(*) FILTER (WHERE v IS NULL), count(*) FILTER (WHERE v = ''), count(*) FILTER (WHERE v = 'NULL') FROM t;
-- 2 | 0 | 1, expected 1 | 1 | 1
```

`EXPORT DATABASE 'out' (FORMAT CSV, NULLSTR 'NULL')` on the same table gives `2 | 0 | 0`: the empty string and the string `'NULL'` both come back as `NULL`.

`test/sql/copy/csv/test_export_not_null.test` already shows the first case: it exports four empty strings and expects the nullable column to come back as `NULL`.

### Cause

`CSVWriter::RequiresQuotes` quotes any value equal to the null string, so the writer emits `""` for an empty string (or `"NULL"` under `NULLSTR 'NULL'`) and a bare marker for `NULL`. The `load.sql` generated by `EXPORT DATABASE` does not set `allow_quoted_nulls false`, so the reader's default of `true` (chosen in #7162 for foreign CSV files) turns the quoted value back into `NULL`.

A second gap makes the `FORMAT CSV` case worse. `EXPORT DATABASE` keeps the format string as written, while `COPY` lowercases it (`bind_copy.cpp`). Both places that add CSV-specific read options compare against `"csv"`, so with `FORMAT CSV` the generated `load.sql` carries neither the `header`, `delimiter` and `quote` defaults nor the `force_not_null` list, and the import falls back to sniffing. On main the `NULLSTR` example above produces `COPY t FROM 't.csv' (FORMAT 'CSV', nullstr 'NULL');`.

### Change

- `WriteCopyStatement` adds `allow_quoted_nulls false` to the `COPY ... FROM` statements it writes for CSV exports, next to the `force_not_null` list it already adds. `allow_quoted_nulls` is a read-only CSV option, so `EXPORT DATABASE` rejects it and there is no user value to override. The reader default does not change.
- `Binder::Bind(ExportStatement)` lowercases the format before the CSV checks, matching `COPY`. `FORMAT CSV` now gets the same `load.sql` options as `FORMAT csv`.

With the change, the first example generates `COPY t FROM 't.csv' (FORMAT 'csv', allow_quoted_nulls false, quote '"', delimiter ',', header 1);` and returns `1 | 1 | 1`.

### Tests

- `test/sql/export/export_quoted_nulls.test` (new) round-trips `NULL`, `''` and `'NULL'` with the default options and, on a two-column table, with `(FORMAT CSV, NULLSTR 'NULL')`, and checks that `load.sql` contains the flag.
- `test/sql/copy/csv/test_export_not_null.test`: the last expected row changes from `(empty) (empty) (empty) NULL` to four `(empty)`.

On main, the new test fails at the `load.sql` check; with that check removed, the default round trip returns `2 | 0 | 1`, and reading the two-column CSV with the options main writes into `load.sql` turns row 3 (`'NULL'`) into a real `NULL`.

### Validation

- `make reldebug` (WSL2, gcc), then `build/reldebug/test/unittest "test/sql/export/*"` (25 cases) and `"test/sql/copy/csv/test_export*"`: all pass.
- `build/reldebug/test/unittest` (fast suite): 6286 cases, 6268 passed, 18 failed. 17 of the failures are CSV sniffing/rejects tests that fail on this Windows-mounted checkout because the CSV fixtures had CRLF line endings; after normalizing the fixtures to LF they all pass (`"test/sql/copy/csv/*"`: 311/312, the remaining one is a symlink-based `.test_slow`). The 18th, `test/sql/secrets/create_secret_filesystem_logging.test`, fails on a secret-file permission check that the mounted filesystem cannot satisfy. None of the 18 use `EXPORT`/`IMPORT DATABASE`.
- `clang-format` 11.0.1 on both changed source files: no changes.
- Not run: `make allunit`, `test_configs`, `test_vector`.

### Notes

Under `NULLSTR 'NULL'`, an empty string in a single-column table is still written as an empty line, which the reader skips as a blank line. That is writer/reader behaviour for blank lines and is unchanged here; the new test uses a two-column table for the `NULLSTR` case so the empty string sits in a field.

title: read_csv('/dev/stdin') accumulates unbounded temp files on large inputs; the same data read by filename streams in constant memory
body:
### What happens?

Reading a large CSV through a pipe with `read_csv('/dev/stdin')` grows memory and
then temp files without bound, until `max_temp_directory_size` (which defaults to
free disk space) is exhausted and the query dies. Handing DuckDB the same data as
a filename instead streams it in constant memory and completes.

I ran into this filtering a private dataset I can't share: a 330 GB CSV
(11 GB gzipped), 1,272,998,467 rows, 8 columns, filtered on the first column
against a list of ids. Between the two runs below, the **only** thing that changed
was the argument to `read_csv`:

| `read_csv` argument | memory | temp used | result |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `'analytics.csv.gz'` | 149-277 MB, flat | **0 bytes** | completes in 3m29s |
| `'/dev/stdin'`, fed by `pigz -dc \|` | ~25 GiB | **80.6 GiB and climbing** | dies |

In the failing run, temp grew at roughly 180 MB/s for the whole run while the
output file stayed at zero bytes, so nothing downstream was completing:

```
t=  0s out=0  temp=
t= 60s out=0  temp=7.8G
t=120s out=0  temp=18G
t=240s out=0  temp=43G
t=360s out=0  temp=69G
t=421s out=0  temp=78G
Out of Memory Error: failed to offload data block of size 256.0 KiB (80.6 GiB/80.6 GiB used).
```

The successful run held **149-277 MB** of memory for its entire duration and
never created a temp file.

Since I can't share that dataset, the section below generates a synthetic CSV of
the same shape that reproduces it.

### Related

This looks like the same problem as
[#12382, "Performance difference with `read_csv` between a file and stdin"](https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb/issues/12382),
which was reported against 1.0.0 at 1M rows and closed. At that scale it presents
as "appears slower". That reporter noted they were considering "ingestion at 100x
the input size"; at roughly 1000x it stops being a slowdown and becomes an
unrecoverable failure that fills the disk.

Worth noting that the piped form is the documented idiom. The
[CSV Import](https://duckdb.org/docs/stable/data/csv/overview) page gives
`cat flights.csv | duckdb -c "SELECT * FROM read_csv('/dev/stdin')"` as the way
to read a CSV from stdin.

### To Reproduce

**1. Generate a large CSV.** The failure scales with input size. I have not
established the smallest input that triggers it; 150M rows (about 26 GB) is well
into the failing range. This takes a few minutes.

```bash
mkdir -p /tmp/repro && cd /tmp/repro
python3 - <<'PY'
import uuid
ua = '"Mozilla/5.0 (X11; Linux) AppleWebKit/537.36 (KHTML, like Gecko)"'
with open('big.csv', 'w') as f:
    f.write("id,a,b,c,d,e\n")
    for i in range(150_000_000):
        f.write(f"{uuid.uuid4()},{uuid.uuid4()},2026-07-01 00:00:00,{ua},10.0.0.{i%256},{i%9}\n")
PY
tail -n +2 big.csv | cut -d, -f1 | head -30 > ids.txt
gzip -c big.csv > big.csv.gz
```

**2. Read it by filename.** Completes, no temp files.

```bash
cd /tmp/repro && rm -rf .tmp out.csv
duckdb -c "COPY (
  SELECT a.* FROM read_csv('big.csv.gz', all_varchar=true) AS a
  WHERE a.id IN (SELECT id FROM read_csv('ids.txt', header=false, columns={'id':'VARCHAR'}))
) TO 'out.csv' (FORMAT CSV, HEADER);"
du -sh .tmp 2>/dev/null || echo "no temp directory created"
```

**3. Read the same bytes through a pipe.** Temp grows without bound.

```bash
cd /tmp/repro && rm -rf .tmp out.csv
gzip -dc big.csv.gz | duckdb -c "COPY (
  SELECT a.* FROM read_csv('/dev/stdin', all_varchar=true) AS a
  WHERE a.id IN (SELECT id FROM read_csv('ids.txt', header=false, columns={'id':'VARCHAR'}))
) TO 'out.csv' (FORMAT CSV, HEADER);"
```

Watch it from another shell while step 3 runs. `.tmp` is DuckDB's default temp
directory for an in-memory database, relative to the working directory:

```bash
while sleep 10; do du -sh /tmp/repro/.tmp 2>/dev/null; done
```

**To fail fast instead of filling the disk**, add a temp cap as the first
statement of the same `-c` string. On my machine this produces the same
`Out of Memory Error` in about 48 seconds rather than several minutes:

```bash
gzip -dc big.csv.gz | duckdb -c "SET max_temp_directory_size='2GiB';
COPY (
  SELECT a.* FROM read_csv('/dev/stdin', all_varchar=true) AS a
  WHERE a.id IN (SELECT id FROM read_csv('ids.txt', header=false, columns={'id':'VARCHAR'}))
) TO 'out.csv' (FORMAT CSV, HEADER);"
```

### What I ruled out

Each of these was tested against the 330 GB dataset and is not the cause.

- **`preserve_insertion_order`.** The error message suggests it. Setting it false
  changes nothing: both settings spill, at the same rate. Reading the same data by
  filename completes with the setting left at its default `true`.
- **Thread count.** `SET threads=1` reading the file completes in 576s with zero
  temp. `SET threads=1` reading the pipe reaches 20 GiB in 149s. Parallel scan
  splitting is not the difference.
- **The output target.** Writing to a plain filename spilled 80.6 GiB; writing to
  `/dev/stdout` spilled 77.0 GiB. Both fail, so it is not the sink.
- **Memory pressure from other processes.** Reproduces on an otherwise idle
  machine. A second DuckDB process competing for memory made it slower, not worse.
- **The temp directory location.** Same behaviour with `temp_directory` at its
  default, pointed at a local disk, and pointed at a network-synced folder.

### Environment

- **DuckDB 1.5.5 (Variegata) d8cdaa33fd**, command-line interface
- macOS 26.5.2, Apple M5, 4 performance + 6 efficiency cores, 32 GiB RAM
- APFS on internal SSD
- Also reproduced on **DuckDB 1.1.3** (Linux x86-64, command-line interface)

### One observation

A gzipped file and stdin are both unseekable, and the documentation treats them
together: samples are taken only from the beginning for "a .gz compressed CSV
file or stdin". Yet the gzipped file streams in 149 MB of memory while stdin
accumulates until the disk is gone. Whatever the reader does differently between
those two cases looks like where the problem is. I have not tried to identify it
beyond confirming that the seekability of the input is the only variable that
changes the outcome.

title: Optimize conflict manager rowid insertion
body: `ConflictManager` is a common data structure used in data insertion when uniqueness required, for example, UNIQUE constraint, primary key, etc. I did some benchmark on data ingestion with `ConflictManager` involved, and I found there's some room we could improve. TLDR: - Currently there're two data structures storing conflict information, one [hashset](https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb/blob/10de9573794001c649621013bdd93553b54e00c9/src/include/duckdb/common/types/conflict_manager.hpp#L145-L146), another is [`ConflictData`](https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb/blob/10de9573794001c649621013bdd93553b54e00c9/src/include/duckdb/common/types/conflict_manager.hpp#L150-L198) - The former, from my understanding, covers the functionality for the hashset (namely, superset), so we could remove the hashset Benchmark script ```sql # name: benchmark/micro/index/point/repeated_fk_lookup_with_art.benchmark # description: Insert repeated foreign keys that hit the same hot ART leaf # group: [point] name Repeated FK Lookup With ART group art load PRAGMA threads=1; CREATE TABLE parent (id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY); INSERT INTO parent VALUES (42); CREATE TABLE input AS SELECT 42::BIGINT AS id FROM range(10000000); CREATE TABLE child (id BIGINT REFERENCES parent(id)); run INSERT INTO child SELECT id FROM input; cleanup DELETE FROM child; ``` From the flamegraph, ~17% CPU is spent on the hashset-related operation Performance change for the benchmark | Metric | Before | After | Improvement | |---|---:|---:|---:| | Mean latency | 1.896 s | 1.510 s | 20.4% | | Median latency | 1.872 s | 1.493 s | 20.2% |

title: Fix CSV reader leaking trailing \n of \r\r\n terminators into next value
body:
Fixes the second symptom reported in #25164 (supplements #25232)

## Problem

Issue #25164 also reports a second symptom on files with `\r\r\n` line
endings: the reader consumes `\r\r` as the row terminator and leaves the
`\n` attached to the front of the first field of the next row (e.g.
symbol arriving as `"\nSPXW"` instead of `"SPXW"`). Unlike the
duplicate-rows bug fixed in #25232, this happens on **sequential reads
too**, and is invisible when the first column is cast to an integer type
(the cast silently trims the `\n`).

## Root cause

With `auto_detect=false` (or mixed-newline files) the scanner runs in
`CARRY_ON` newline mode, where five sites advance the value start
position by a hard-coded 2 bytes — written for 2-byte `"\r\n"`
terminators. With a 3-byte `"\r\r\n"` terminator the leftover `"\n"`
lands on the start of the next value, both when the terminator is fully
inside one buffer and when a buffer boundary splits it as `"\r" |
"\r\n"` or `"\r\r" | "\n"`.

## Fix

Make those sites aware of the 3-byte terminator:
- `AddRow` / `UnsetComment`: when the bytes after the terminator are
  `"\r\r\n"`, skip 3 instead of 2
- `ProcessOverBufferValue`: after consuming the remaining `"\r\n"` of a
  split terminator, refresh `last_position` to point past it (both
  early-return paths, including the double-count guard added in #25232)
- `ProcessOverBufferValue`: start the next value after a
  boundary-leading newline and never append leading newline bytes to a
  pending value

## Testing

New regression test `test/sql/copy/csv/test_rrrn_leading_newline.test`
(uses VARCHAR ids so the leak is assertable): three layouts — all rows
in a single buffer, boundary splitting as `"\r" | "\r\n"`, and as

title: Fix filter pushdown for table in-out functions
fix: Integer Truncation in approx_k_values() leading to heap buffer overflow
body:
Fixes https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb/issues/25575

## Summary
`CopyValue()` rounded a strings size up to the next power of two, then truncated that result into a `uint32_t` via `UnsafeNumericCast` before allocating. For strings sized in (2^31, 2^32-1], the rounded size is exactly 2^32, which wraps to 0 on truncation. This made Allocate(0) return a zero byte buffer while the following memcpy still copied the full string into it.

## Fix
Widened `ApproxTopKValue::capacity` from `uint32_t` to `idx_t` and removed the truncating `UnsafeNumericCast<uint32_t>` around the power of two calculation.
The allocator now always receives the correctly computed size.
Oversized allocations now cleanly fail through DuckDBs normal `OutOfMemoryException` path instead of corrupting the heap.

## Test
`test_approx_top_k_overflow.test_slow`: produces a string leading to `2^32` rounding case and it will hit a clean Out of Memory error.

title: Table-in/out functions silently drop predicates when filter_pushdown is enabled
body:
### What happens?

A table-in/out function that sets `TableFunction::filter_pushdown = true` cannot receive the pushed `TableFilterSet`. DuckDB's filter-pushdown optimizer can move an eligible predicate into `LogicalGet::table_filters` and remove the residual filter, but the table-in/out physical-planning path then drops that filter state. The function therefore cannot fulfill the filter-pushdown contract, and the query can return unfiltered rows.

This is a correctness issue rather than only a missed optimization.

The relevant core path at commit `70e7a857595b5872842b6ec242ac79c182e58dde` is:

1. `FilterPushdown::PushdownGet` generates `LogicalGet::table_filters` when `get.function.filter_pushdown` is true:
   https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb/blob/70e7a857595b5872842b6ec242ac79c182e58dde/src/optimizer/pushdown/pushdown_get.cpp#L113-L160
2. `PhysicalPlanGenerator::CreatePlan(LogicalGet &op)` takes the `op.children` table-in/out branch and returns a `PhysicalTableInOutFunction` before the normal `MoveTableFilters` path:
   https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb/blob/70e7a857595b5872842b6ec242ac79c182e58dde/src/execution/physical_plan/plan_get.cpp#L33-L85
3. `PhysicalTableInOutFunction` constructs both global and local `TableFunctionInitInput` with `nullptr` filters:
   https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb/blob/70e7a857595b5872842b6ec242ac79c182e58dde/src/execution/operator/projection/physical_tableinout_function.cpp#L44-L70

This is consistent with the contract clarified in #19818: after setting `filter_pushdown`, the table function is expected to handle the pushed table filters. A table-in/out function currently has no opportunity to do that.

Expected behavior: predicates accepted into `LogicalGet::table_filters` and based solely on the table-in/out function's output should either be provided through `TableFunctionInitInput::filters` or retained as residual filters. They should never be silently discarded.

This issue is intentionally not requesting any change to correlated-filter semantics. Predicates involving columns from the input child should continue to follow their existing behavior.

### To Reproduce

Register a minimal table-in/out function that echoes an integer input column and advertises filter pushdown:

```cpp
TableFunction function("filter_probe", {LogicalType::TABLE}, nullptr, Bind, GlobalInit, LocalInit);
function.in_out_function = EchoInput;
function.filter_pushdown = true;
```

Have `GlobalInit` and/or `LocalInit` inspect `TableFunctionInitInput::filters`, and execute:

```sql
SELECT value
FROM filter_probe((SELECT i::INTEGER AS value FROM range(3) t(i)))
WHERE value = 1;
```

The pushed predicate is present on the optimized `LogicalGet`, but both initialization callbacks receive `input.filters == nullptr`. Because the optimizer trusted the function to apply the predicate, no residual filter remains and the echo function returns:

```text
0
1
2
```

The expected result is:

```text
1
```

A standalone compiled reproducer needs the usual table-function registration and callback boilerplate; the three core paths linked above show where the filter is moved and then omitted.

title: Fix OOB read in SortedAggregateBindData reconstruction (#25281)
body:
### Problem

The problem was calling `finalize(to_aggregate_state(...))` on an ordered aggregate state whose declared argument signature had more entries than the buffered values struct fields causes an OOB read. I reproduceced it in debug/ASan build and it aborts with a memory safety error. However, in a release build it silently reads past the end of the `buffered_types` vector (reading garbage memory is dangerous).

fixes and closes https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb/issues/25281

**Repro:**

```sql
SELECT finalize(to_aggregate_state([{'v0': 1}], 'string_agg', ['VARCHAR','VARCHAR'], NULL, [{'column': 0, 'order': 'ASC NULLS FIRST'}]));
```

Here the buffered value `{'v0': 1}` has 1 field, but the declared signature (`['VARCHAR','VARCHAR']`) implies 2 arguments. These two were not validated beforehand and were assumed to be matching before `SortedAggregateBindData`'s reconstruction constructor indexed into `buffered_types` up to `argument_count`.

### Root Cause

`BindAggregateStateInternal` (in `src/function/scalar/system/aggregate_export.cpp`) derives `column_count` from the buffer struct's actual shape and `argument_count` from the inner aggregate's bound arguments, then passes both to `FunctionBinder::BindSortedAggregateState` without checking `argument_count <= column_count`. I also checked the existing `ParseOrderBys`  already validates  `column` index against `column_count`  but this same validation was not present for `argument_count`.

### Fix

Instead of validating  in `SortedAggregateBindData`'s constructor  I added a bounds check in `BindAggregateStateInternal`, right after `argument_count` is computed and before it's used to construct the sorted aggregate wrapper.

This throws `BinderException` and does not let a invalid arguments to reach `SortedAggregateBindData`'s constructor.

### Testing

Added `test/sql/aggregate/aggregate_state_export/test_sorted_aggregate_state_bounds.test`:

- A `statement error` case reproducing the original OOB scenario, showing it throws  `BinderException` now.
- A `query` case confirming a valid case where `argument_count` matches buffered struct  is correct.
Ran the new test in isolation and the broader `test/sql/aggregate/aggregate_state_export/*` suite to confirm no regressions.

###summary

Fixes out of bound read in `SortedAggregateBindData` reconstruction, where `BindAggregateStateInternal` computed `argument_count` and the buffered struct's actual field count independently and never validated with each other allowing `finalize(to_aggregate_state(...))` to index past the end of a vector on specific inputs. Added a validation check that throws a clean `BinderException` instead, plus a  test covering both the bug and a valid case.

### Notes for reviewers

This is my first pull request here. Please let me know if there is any thing wrong with the PR or any kind of issues.
Thankyou for your attention.

title: Skip all-NULL partitions and add BOOLEAN to MIN/MAX folding
body:
Hi team!

This extends the basic MIN/MAX path: an all-NULL partition is now treated as neutral instead of vetoing the fold, and BOOLEAN columns can be folded from row group statistics.

`min`/`max` orders each partition's surviving values, so a partition that holds only NULLs cannot affect the extremum - but the basic path treated the absence of min/max stats as a reason to abandon the rewrite for the whole table. BOOLEAN also keeps its min/max in the numeric statistics, but `LogicalType::IsNumeric()` does not cover it, so `GetComparator()` returned nothing and the rewrite bailed.

`TryFoldMinMaxAggregates` now returns `PartitionValueOutcome` with four states (VALUE / ALL_NULL / BOUND / NO_INFO). ALL_NULL is consumed by the fold; BOUND and NO_INFO both keep abandoning the rewrite for now - BOUND is the slot the scan-and-merge path will fill once it is reachable.

title: WAL group commit
body:
# WAL group commit via bounded snapshots

## Summary

A commit currently fsyncs the WAL while holding both the WAL lock and the commit path's locks, so concurrent committers queue behind each other's fsyncs and throughput is pinned near `1 / fsync_latency` regardless of how many connections are committing. That is most painful on high-latency durable storage — networked disks, where a single fsync can take milliseconds to seconds — and it is exactly the situation where batching helps most.

This PR keeps the publish where it is and moves the fsync *after* the locks are released whenever other transactions exist, where concurrent commits share it: one sync leader fsyncs the WAL up to the highest marker any committer has requested, everyone else waits, and each commit is acknowledged once its own marker is durable. The durability contract is unchanged — nothing acknowledged can be lost to a crash — but one fsync now covers a whole group of commits.

At 1 ms of fsync latency and 32 committers this takes the same workload from **1.23 s to 0.039 s — about 32x**, and the advantage widens with concurrency because larger groups amortise each fsync over more commits.

## What this builds on

#25187 states the snapshot visibility rule once: a transaction reads at a `VisibilityBound`, carried in its `SnapshotView`. #25389 lets `DuckTransaction` own that view and factors the lowest-bound computation and the committed sweep out of `RemoveTransaction`. Both are behaviour-neutral and are merged on `v2.0-cyanoptera`; this PR targets `main` and is based on it once they have been merged in. On top of them it only has to cap the bound where the view is built, and pin the lowest bound while commits are pending durability.

## Why this is safe: bounded snapshots

Main is *already* publish-then-fsync: `undo_buffer.Commit` makes the changes visible and `FlushCommit` fsyncs afterwards. It is safe there only because the locks block every observer for the duration of the fsync. Moving the fsync out of the locks removes that protection, so something has to replace it.

Rather than defer the publish, this PR bounds what new transactions may *observe*. While commits are pending durability, `StartTransaction` caps a new snapshot's visibility bound below the first commit that is not yet durable, so no transaction can see a commit a crash could still lose. Acknowledging a commit advances the bound, which means read-your-writes still holds: once `COMMIT` returns, that commit is durable and every subsequently started transaction sees it. A transaction that started *during* the window may not see it — but it began before the commit was acknowledged, so it was never entitled to.

This is the whole safety argument, and it is why the publish and the registration of the pending commit happen inside a single uninterrupted hold of the transaction lock, which `StartTransaction` must also take: there is no instant at which a commit is visible but unbounded.

## How it works

- **The WAL sync splits in two.** `FlushMarker` writes the `WAL_FLUSH` marker and pushes the buffer to the OS, still under the WAL lock; `SyncUpTo(offset)` runs after the locks are released and blocks until the WAL is durable to that offset, electing one caller as the leader on behalf of every offset requested so far.
- **Sync offsets are logical, not file positions.** A truncation rewinds the file and a later marker can reuse an offset, so file positions are ambiguous across truncation. `BufferedFileWriter::GetTotalWritten` never rewinds, so a logical offset is never reused and a sync that spans a truncation is simply correct — no generation counter, no clamping.
- **Pending commits stay active.** A committed transaction remains in `active_transactions` until its WAL sync completes, carrying its flush-marker offset and the catalog version just before it published. The durable bound advances offset-based by whichever thread's sync covered a commit, so an acknowledgement always implies observability, and `WaitForDurability` waits until no active transaction still awaits its sync, which checkpoints use before swapping or deleting the WAL.
- **A commit with no other transaction syncs under the transaction lock**, as on main. There is nothing to share the fsync with, no snapshot can be bounded below it, and the index fast path that skips `deleted_rows_in_use` stays available to it; the deferred, shared sync is used only by commits that overlap other transactions.
- **Retention needs no special case.** A pending commit holds the lowest visibility bound like any active transaction, so nothing a bounded snapshot might still read is vacuumed, and `HasOtherTransactions` counts it without being told.
- **Bounded transactions cap their catalog version too.** Bind state created under a bounded snapshot — a prepared statement re-bound during the window resolves to the pre-commit catalog entry — must not be stamped with a version later transactions would trust.
- **Checkpoints drain first.** The checkpoint's visibility transaction starts only after the drain, and the decision paths that assumed a fresh snapshot starts above the last commit re-validate against bounded snapshots.
- **A failed shared fsync invalidates the database.** A commit that synced alone, under the transaction lock, rolls back as on main. Later syncs of that WAL fail fast, so every commit still awaiting its sync leaves the active set promptly and no drain hangs. The commits whose sync failed stay in the WAL, so a restart may replay them: they are in doubt, like any commit whose acknowledgement was lost.

## Benchmark

`benchmark/micro/concurrent_commits.cpp` (`[wal]`): concurrent single-row-commit throughput on a persistent database at real, 1 ms and 10 ms fsync latency, with the latency injected through a `LocalFileSystem` subclass on the DB config. Fixed total work per latency tier, so wall time falls as more commits share each fsync. Median of 5; this PR, with `main` in parentheses; lower is better.

| threads         | real fsync     | 1 ms            | 10 ms           |
| --------------- | -------------: | --------------: | --------------: |
| 1 (no batching) | 2.58 s (2.46)  | 1.74 s (1.75)   | 2.27 s (2.25)   |
| 4               | 0.91 s (0.97)  | 0.63 s (1.37)   | 1.05 s (2.14)   |
| 8               | 0.74 s (0.94)  | 0.34 s (1.36)   | 0.54 s (2.15)   |
| 16              | 0.74 s (0.95)  | 0.16 s (1.34)   | 0.28 s (2.13)   |
| 32              | 0.76 s (0.96)  | 0.080 s (1.38)  | 0.14 s (2.14)   |

`main` is invariant to concurrency: it sits at `1 / fsync_latency` whether 1 or 32 threads are committing. This PR scales with committer count: at 1 ms fsync latency, 4 threads finish 2.2x faster than on `main`, 8 threads 4.0x, 16 threads 8.4x and 32 threads 17x, with the same shape at 10 ms. One sync runs at a time, so a commit arriving during a sync waits for it and joins the next; per-commit latency stays between one and two fsyncs, and the throughput comes from every sync covering all commits flushed since the previous one. Single-threaded is at parity: with nothing to batch, each commit still pays its own fsync. Single-threaded write microbenchmarks, 20k autocommit inserts, a 5M-row bulk load, 20k autocommit updates and 20k autocommit deletes on an indexed table, are all within noise of main. The real-fsync column plateaus past the core count on a fast local SSD, where there is nothing left to amortise; its 20% gain at 8+ threads comes from the fsync no longer running under the commit locks. The latency columns are the point.

## Testing

Beyond the usual suites, three things are worth calling out.

**The new invariants are pinned by tests that fail without them.** Deleting the snapshot cap outright, or removing a committed transaction from the active set before its sync completes, each left the entire suite green when this work started: the stress tests assert aggregates after all threads have joined, which the cap does not affect. `test/api/test_group_commit_bound.cpp` asserts the bound directly, parking a commit inside its WAL fsync with a gated file system so the interleaving is deterministic: a transaction starting in that window does not see the commit, does not see it on a second read either (including across another connection's rollback, which drains the cleanup queue), still conflicts with it, and two such transactions report distinct `txid_current()` values. Each of those mutations now fails one of these tests.

**Fault injection.** `debug_wal_fsync_sleep_ms` and `debug_force_wal_fsync_failure` inject latency and failures into the sync leader. The delay widens the publish-to-durable window for the SQL stress tests; the failure switch covers the poisoning path, including a group where one leader's fsync fails and no committer in it may be acknowledged.

**Crash durability.** A kill -9 harness confirms across 12 rounds that every acknowledged commit survives crash and replay, plus 8 rounds for the optimistic-write path, and again with a 10 ms fsync delay so the publish-to-durable window is wide.

New SQL tests cover conflicting commits, unique-key races, concurrent checkpoints, DDL concurrent with group commit, and a failed shared fsync.

## Behaviour changes worth flagging

**A failed WAL fsync can invalidate the database.** On main the fsync happens inside the revertable window, so an `EIO`/`ENOSPC` surfaces as a failed commit on a still-usable database. That is still the case for a commit that syncs alone: with no other transaction to share the fsync with, it syncs under the transaction lock and a failure rolls it back. A commit that shares its sync has already published and released its locks when the fsync fails, so it cannot be undone: the database is invalidated. This is the most user-visible change in the PR and belongs in the release notes.

A commit whose shared sync failed is in doubt. Its bytes reached the OS before the fsync failed, so a restart may replay it even though `COMMIT` reported an error, the same outcome any database has for a commit whose acknowledgement was lost. On main the failed fsync is reverted inside the commit and leaves nothing behind; an earlier version of this PR truncated the never-durable tail to keep that, at the cost of tracking file positions alongside the logical sync offsets. That bookkeeping is gone: the in-doubt contract is the simpler one, and it holds whether or not the process survives the failure.

**Wider exposure to torn WAL tails (pre-existing, not introduced).** DuckDB treats a WAL checksum mismatch as corruption rather than end-of-log, so a zero-filled tail — what unordered writeback produces after a crash — makes the database unopenable. That is true on `main` and here alike (verified on both); what changes is that the never-synced tail grows from at most one commit to a whole group. Clean truncation mid-entry still recovers as a prefix. Treating a checksum failure as end-of-log, as SQLite and Postgres do, would remove the class entirely, but that is a recovery-policy change for its own PR.

**`CHECKPOINT` can wait on another connection's fsync.** The drain runs under the WAL lock, where no new commit can enter its sync window, so it is bounded by the syncs already in flight rather than by how busy the writers are.

## Not included

Commits that checkpoint instead of writing the WAL still hold the WAL lock across the checkpoint, exactly as on main; we can look at that separately later. The `UPDATE_TUPLE`-vs-ALTER atomicity gap (pre-existing issue) is untouched — it reproduces without any of this work and needs its own fix.

title: Fix header handling in CSV minimal sniff
body: Hi team, when I read through the CSV schema sniff code, I found when multiple files involved, we seem to degrade from happy path [minimal sniff](https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb/blob/10de9573794001c649621013bdd93553b54e00c9/src/execution/operator/csv_scanner/sniffer/csv_sniffer.cpp#L147) to the fallback slow path [full sniff](https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb/blob/10de9573794001c649621013bdd93553b54e00c9/src/execution/operator/csv_scanner/sniffer/csv_sniffer.cpp#L159). ### Problem statement The issue is - During binding, schema discovery runs the full CSV sniffer on the first file, then on additional files until it has sampled at least 20,480 rows in total or reached 10 files, and merges the resulting schemas. - [`MinimalSniff`](https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb/blob/10de9573794001c649621013bdd93553b54e00c9/src/execution/operator/csv_scanner/sniffer/csv_sniffer.cpp#L80) is called in [`AdaptiveSniff`](https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb/blob/10de9573794001c649621013bdd93553b54e00c9/src/execution/operator/csv_scanner/sniffer/csv_sniffer.cpp#L146), which used to decide whether all CSV files match the discovered schema - In the current implementation, MinimalSniff will likely [set start row as 0](https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb/blob/10de9573794001c649621013bdd93553b54e00c9/src/execution/operator/csv_scanner/sniffer/csv_sniffer.cpp#L108-L112), so header (all columns `VARCHAR`) is used as type, which likely disagrees with the discovered schema and falls back to full schema detection for all file Pseudocode here: ```sh minimal_result = MinimalSniff(); if (minimal_result matches known_schema) { return minimal_result; // fast path } return SniffCSV(); // sniff all csvs ``` Difference between fast path and full sniff - For the minimal sniff fast path, we only need to validate whether the discovered schema matches csv rows - While in the full sniff path, we also need to detect dialect, detect type, detect header, etc ### Background investigation I checked the git commit, it reads to me that once upon a time, we were using the first two rows to decide schema, that's where the if statement `start_position == 2` comes from. Related PR: https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb/pull/13703, which switches the number of rows to detect schema from 2 to `VECTOR_SIZE`. ### Performance evaluation I wrote a benchmark to evaluate the performance gain for this change ```sql # name: benchmark/csv/multi_file_adaptive_sniff.benchmark # description: Measure adaptive schema sniffing over many small CSV files # group: [csv] name CSV Multi-File Adaptive Sniff Benchmark group csv load CREATE TABLE csv_files AS SELECT file_id, row_id::BIGINT AS id, DATE '2026-01-01' + row_id::INTEGER AS event_date, (row_id * 1.5)::DOUBLE AS amount FROM range(500) files(file_id), range(3) rows(row_id); COPY csv_files TO '${BENCHMARK_DIR}/adaptive_sniff' (FORMAT CSV, PARTITION_BY ('file_id'), HEADER, OVERWRITE_OR_IGNORE TRUE); init SET threads=1; run SELECT count(*) FROM read_csv('${BENCHMARK_DIR}/adaptive_sniff/**/*.csv', hive_partitioning=false); result I 1500 ``` Benchmark result | Release Build | Median Time | Relative Performance | |---|---:|---:| | Before fix | 78.6 ms | 1.00× | | After fix | 32.9 ms | 2.39× faster |

title: Fix temp file deadloop
body:
DuckDB spills in-memory block to disk when memory threshold reaches and temp directory configured.
To prevent concurrent access, we acquire a file lock identified by [PID and instance id](https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb/blob/70e7a857595b5872842b6ec242ac79c182e58dde/src/storage/temporary_file_manager.cpp#L722-L724); when it's been acquired by someone else we busyloop until lock released.

But with current implementation, we [retry on whatever exception](https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb/blob/70e7a857595b5872842b6ec242ac79c182e58dde/src/storage/temporary_file_manager.cpp#L846-L848), even if the marker file doesn't exist, which could lead to unnecessary indefinite loop. For example,
```sh
[~/Desktop/duckdb (v2.0-cyanoptera)]
haojiang@HaoJiangs-MacBook-Pro$ mkdir /tmp/rodir-hjiang && chmod 555 /tmp/rodir-hjiang 

[~/Desktop/duckdb (v2.0-cyanoptera)] 
haojiang@HaoJiangs-MacBook-Pro$ ./build/reldebug/duckdb
DuckDB v2.0.0-dev84402 (Development Version, 88902aaa39)
Enter ".help" for usage hints.
memory D PRAGMA memory_limit='48MB';
memory D PRAGMA temp_directory='/tmp/rodir';
memory D SET preserve_insertion_order=false;
memory D CREATE TABLE big AS SELECT range a, md5(range::VARCHAR) b FROM range(800000);
memory D SELECT count(*) FROM (SELECT b, count(*) FROM big GROUP BY b) t; 
-- stall, should throw exception directly
```
In this PR, I update the retry criteria to only attempt on non-existent files.

title: Defer foreign key constraint validation until the end of the statement
body:
Fixes #7168, #10574, #24215, #16785.

Foreign keys are currently checked while a statement is still executing (per chunk in the insert sinks), before the rows of that chunk have been appended. A statement that inserts multiple rows into a self-referencing table therefore fails, even though all referenced rows exist by the end of the statement. The same early checking makes statements that write multiple tables depend on pipeline execution order: COPY FROM DATABASE is a single statement with one INSERT per table, and whether it succeeds depends on the table order and on parallel pipeline execution.

Issue relations: #7168 and #10574 are the same problem on a single table (#10574 is batch loading into a self-referencing table). #24215 reports the same failure as the original #16785 report; the thread of #16785 additionally contains a self-referencing FK variant, which is covered by the same change.

This PR defers the check to the end of the statement:

- The FK case is removed from the eager per-chunk VerifyAppendConstraints (NOT NULL / CHECK / UNIQUE remain eager).
- Transaction-local storage records the row range each statement appended (statement = query number, range = local row positions), in the two functions through which appends enter local storage (LocalStorage::Append and LocalStorage::LocalMerge).
- Once a statement has finished executing (all pipelines completed, before any commit), the client context verifies the foreign keys for the rows that statement appended. Only the foreign key columns are read, in batches of STANDARD_VECTOR_SIZE rows, so memory stays bounded; no pipeline ordering is needed for foreign keys.
- The key columns are read back from transaction-local storage with a range scan over the appended rows (vectorized, only the FK key columns); index construction already read these columns at the end of the insert, so this is usually cache-warm.
- Nothing is buffered or copied - the rows already live in transaction-local storage, and only the appended row range is tracked.
- Verification runs before the commit decision, and a foreign key violation is reported as a statement error through the existing error path.
- Appends made while no statement is running (the internal appender can be used that way) keep their eager checks, since there is no statement end to defer to. When the internal appender is used during a statement, its appends are deferred like any other.
- Catalogs whose transaction objects are not DuckDB transactions (storage extensions) are skipped during verification, so attaching such a catalog does not interfere with statement execution.

Not covered by this PR:

- DELETE/TRUNCATE-side statement-level visibility (#13819).

Performance (release build, Apple M3):

- benchmark/micro/index/insert/insert_pk_fk.benchmark (in-memory, three foreign keys): median 310.4 ms -> 314 ms (+0.7%). An earlier version read the key columns back row by row and showed +17.9% (310.4 ms -> 365.8 ms) on the same benchmark.
- Largest overhead we measured: inserting 6M rows of TPC-H SF1 lineitem into a 16-column table with one foreign key, on a file-backed database where completed row groups are written to disk and compressed while the insert runs: +8-14%.
- insert_pk_fk.benchmark is not part of .github/regression/micro.csv, so CI does not run this workload today.

Tests:

- new: test/sql/constraints/foreignkey/fk_statement_level_validation.test (+ _slow), and test/api/test_appender_api.cpp "Test internal appender foreign key checks"
- new: test/api/test_storage_extension_alias.cpp "Statements executed while a non-DuckDB catalog is attached"
- un-skipped: test/sql/copy_database/copy_database_fk.test (previously "mode skip instable" with an FK ordering FIXME) now passes
- updated expectations: test_fk_self_referencing.test and foreign_key_matching_columns.test. A row may now reference itself, which is consistent with statement-level visibility (SQLite allows this as well); both tests encoded the previous, earlier checking behavior.

title: Fix collation handling for DISTINCT aggregates (part 1)
body:
Fixes #24319 

# Overview

This PR fixes collation handling for grouped and ungrouped `DISTINCT` aggregates by applying collation-aware comparison during the multi-stage aggregate rewrite. So, values such as `Apple` and `apple` are treated as equal under `NOCASE`. By applying collation to the rewrite’s grouping keys, DuckDB can reuse its existing collation-aware `GROUP BY` machinery instead of adding separate collation logic to the physical `DISTINCT` operators.

The rewrite converts a `DISTINCT` aggregate into an ordinary aggregate over a deduplicated input. The deduplication groups by the normalized comparison key, while hidden `first(...)` aggregates preserve an original representative for aggregates that return values such as `LIST(DISTINCT name)`.

# Implementation details

`CreateDistinctBranch` now builds deduplication branches using collation-aware comparison keys. Each `DISTINCT` child is copied and rebound to the branch input, then passed through `PushCollation` when necessary. The resulting normalized expressions become grouping keys.

When a child is normalized, the rewrite also creates a hidden `first(...)` aggregate over the original expression. The final aggregate consumes this representative instead of the normalized key, preserving the original value returned by aggregates like `LIST(DISTINCT name)`.

`DISTINCT` aggregates may share a deduplication branch only when their children, filters, ordering expressions, and collation metadata are compatible. This prevents expressions with different comparison semantics from incorrectly sharing state.

`ORDER BY` expressions are handled separately from `DISTINCT` children when necessary. Collation metadata is included when matching aggregate arguments to ordering keys, ensuring that expressions such as `name COLLATE NOCASE` and `name COLLATE C` are stored and ordered independently.

The new collation helpers compare and hash collation metadata recursively, including nested types such as lists, arrays, maps, structs, and unions. `ClientContext` is passed through the relevant binding paths because collation resolution and hidden aggregate binding require query and database state.

# Out of scope

When the optimizer is disabled, the multi-stage rewrite does not run and DuckDB falls back to the existing physical `DISTINCT` implementation. Collation handling in that fallback path remains a transition limitation and is outside the scope of this PR.

This PR does not cover window DISTINCT aggregates, UNIQUE or PRIMARY KEY constraints, or make the multi-stage rewrite mandatory.

title: C API returns incorrect values when reading Constant NULL list children
body:
### What happens?

The DuckDB C API can return incorrect values when reading a LIST child backed by a Constant NULL vector.

For example, a C API extension reading the child vector by logical index returns:

```sql
SELECT dfn_echo_list_integer_n([NULL, NULL, NULL, NULL]);
```

```text
[NULL, 0, 0, 0]
```

instead of:

```text
[NULL, NULL, NULL, NULL]
```

The non-NULL values are garbage data and can differ between process runs.

Reproduced with DuckDB v1.5.4 and v1.5.5.


### To Reproduce

The attached extension is a small test extension that exposes the issue through the DuckDB C API.

The extension is built for multiple platforms by this GitHub Actions workflow:

[Build artifacts / GitHub Actions run](https://github.com/shijianjs/duckfn/actions/runs/34605792321)

The relevant source code is here:

[duck_list_scalar_echo.rs](https://github.com/shijianjs/duckfn/blob/b9c144ec337094a6d4665410d70220f99f90400d/src/extension/types/duck_list_scalar_echo.rs#L114)

The full LIST implementation is somewhat large, so I have not included it inline.

Load the extension and run:

```sql
SELECT dfn_echo_list_integer_n([NULL, NULL, NULL, NULL]);
```

Actual result:

```text
[NULL, 0, 0, 0]
```

Expected result:

```text
[NULL, NULL, NULL, NULL]
```

The value `0` is not deterministic; different process runs can produce different values.

The same issue occurs with an explicitly typed list:

```sql
SELECT dfn_echo_list_integer_n([NULL, NULL, NULL, NULL]::INTEGER[]);
```

Actual:

```text
[NULL, 0, 0, 0]
```

However, specifying the type of just one element avoids the issue:

```sql
SELECT dfn_echo_list_integer_n(
    [NULL, NULL::INTEGER, NULL, NULL]
);
-- [NULL, NULL, NULL, NULL]
```

```sql
SELECT dfn_echo_list_integer_n(
    [NULL, NULL, NULL::INTEGER, NULL]
);
-- [NULL, NULL, NULL, NULL]
```

Typing all elements also works:

```sql
SELECT dfn_echo_list_integer_n(
    [NULL::INTEGER, NULL::INTEGER, NULL::INTEGER, NULL::INTEGER]
);
-- [NULL, NULL, NULL, NULL]
```

The issue appears to be specific to SQL literals whose elements are all untyped `NULL`. Passing the value through a relation or producing it through an actual computation does not reproduce it.

Regular constant values are unaffected:

```sql
SELECT dfn_echo_list_integer_n([1, 1, 1, 1]);
-- [1, 1, 1, 1]
```

The same behavior can also be reproduced for MAP values:

```sql
SELECT dfn_echo_map_varchar_integer_n(
    map(['a', 'b'], [NULL, NULL])
);
-- {a=NULL, b=0}
```

### Suspected cause

For `[NULL, NULL, NULL, NULL]`, the LIST child appears to remain a Constant NULL vector. Its logical length is 4, but its physical data buffer contains only one element.

DuckDB's internal `UnifiedVectorFormat` handles this representation by mapping all logical indices to the same physical element.

The C API exposes `duckdb_vector_get_data()` and `duckdb_vector_get_validity()`, but does not expose the vector representation or an equivalent logical-index access mechanism.

The extension therefore reads the data buffer using the logical index. Index 0 is handled as NULL, while subsequent indices access beyond the physical buffer.

Is this expected C API behavior? If so, what is the intended way for a C API extension to safely read such a nested vector?

title: v2 C API: table functions can only be scanned by one thread
Arrow scan: estimated cardinality is always 1, so `ORDER BY ... LIMIT` loses `TOP_N`
body:
### What happens?

For a registered Arrow table, the estimated cardinality that reaches the optimizer is always 1, and
it arrives flagged as a known estimate rather than as absent. This degrades optimizer decisions (ie: TopN selection) for arrow sources. 

## Impact
The estimate is *wrong and flagged as known*, so the optimizer trusts it and plans for a one-row table.

The cheapest demonstration, on a 2,000,000-row `pa.Table` in duckdb-python, changing one character:

```
SELECT * FROM arrow_tbl ORDER BY price DESC LIMIT 5000   ->  TOP_N      7.2 ms
SELECT * FROM arrow_tbl ORDER BY price DESC LIMIT 5001   ->  ORDER_BY  50.4 ms
```

**7x for one extra row of limit.** Above a limit of 5000 the planner decides a full sort beats a
top-N on what it believes is a one-row input. The same query over a native table of the same rows is
unaffected at both limits. Anyone running `ORDER BY ... LIMIT` over a registered `pa.Table`, or a
pandas frame that arrives through Arrow, pays this today, with no error and nothing in the plan that
looks obviously wrong unless you read the row estimate.

Top-N is only where it is easiest to see. The same 1 is what the join order optimizer reads when it
picks join order and build sides, so every cardinality-driven decision over Arrow data is made
against a one-row input.

## Solutions

* **Engine side: give the planner a way to say "unknown".** `TopN::CanOptimize` already branches on
  `has_estimated_cardinality`, so an absent estimate would keep `TOP_N`. Nothing reaches that branch,
  because `EstimateCardinality` returns a plain `idx_t` and cannot express absence
* **Producer side: let a source that knows its count say so.** An optional `estimated_rows` parameter on `arrow_scan`. 

## Explanation / Analysis

#### `ArrowScanCardinality` returns an empty `NodeStatistics`
https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb/blob/625f75fce87c7b49c0bef7c331bd89a32d1c0d38/src/function/table/arrow.cpp#L216-L218

#### `LogicalGet::EstimateCardinality` falls past its `function.cardinality` branch to the literal `return 1` at the end
https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb/blob/625f75fce87c7b49c0bef7c331bd89a32d1c0d38/src/planner/operator/logical_get.cpp#L274-L289

#### `LogicalOperator::EstimateCardinality` stamps that 1 on the `ORDER_BY` node with `has_estimated_cardinality = true`
https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb/blob/625f75fce87c7b49c0bef7c331bd89a32d1c0d38/src/planner/logical_operator.cpp#L261-L273

#### `TopN::CanOptimize` then runs its heuristic against that 1
https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb/blob/625f75fce87c7b49c0bef7c331bd89a32d1c0d38/src/optimizer/topn_optimizer.cpp#L41-L54

In a real query the stamping happens earlier still: the join order optimizer runs first and calls
`get.EstimateCardinality(context)` then `get.SetEstimatedCardinality(...)`
(https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb/blob/625f75fce87c7b49c0bef7c331bd89a32d1c0d38/src/optimizer/join_order/relation_manager.cpp#L552-L565),
so the 1 is already baked in by the time `TopN` runs.

`limit > child_card * 0.007` is true for every limit when `child_card` is 1, so the decision reduces
to `limit > 5000` (`constant_limit` includes any OFFSET). An Arrow table still gets `TOP_N` at
limits of 5000 and below, and loses it above that, however many rows it actually holds.

The row estimate and the resulting plan, for 2,000,000 rows and `LIMIT 10000`:

| source | row estimate | plan |
| --- | --- | --- |
| native table | ~2,000,000 | `TOP_N` |
| registered Arrow table | **~1** | `ORDER_BY` |

Injecting a cardinality locally, changing nothing else, flips the Arrow arm to `TOP_N`, so the
estimate is the whole cause.

### To Reproduce


The patch below adds `test/arrow/arrow_topn.cpp`, modelled on the existing
`test/arrow/arrow_filter_pushdown.cpp`, which already builds an `arrow_scan` and reads its
`EXPLAIN`. It scans the same 2,000,000 rows two ways and compares the plans.

The native arm passes. The Arrow arm fails, and the message carries both row estimates:

```
test/arrow/arrow_topn.cpp:63: FAILED:
  REQUIRE( PlanKind(arrow_explain) == "TOP_N" )
with expansion:
  "ORDER_BY" == "TOP_N"
with message:
  arrow scan estimate: ~1, native estimate: ~2,000,000
```

diff --git a/test/arrow/CMakeLists.txt b/test/arrow/CMakeLists.txt
index d38dc7718f..39432c005c 100644
--- a/test/arrow/CMakeLists.txt
+++ b/test/arrow/CMakeLists.txt
@@ -5,6 +5,7 @@ add_library_unity(
   arrow_roundtrip.cpp
   arrow_move_children.cpp
   arrow_filter_pushdown.cpp
+  arrow_topn.cpp
   arrow_dictionary_sentinel.cpp
   arrow_dict_nested_offset.cpp
   arrow_list_view_nested_offset.cpp
diff --git a/test/arrow/arrow_topn.cpp b/test/arrow/arrow_topn.cpp
new file mode 100644
index 0000000000..b595962a8b
--- /dev/null
+++ b/test/arrow/arrow_topn.cpp
@@ -0,0 +1,64 @@
+#include "catch.hpp"
+
+#include "arrow/arrow_test_helper.hpp"
+
+using namespace duckdb;
+
+// An ArrowTestFactory over the rows a query returns, which arrow_scan can then scan.
+static unique_ptr<ArrowTestFactory> MakeArrowFactory(Connection &con, const string &query) {
+	auto client_properties = con.context->GetClientProperties();
+	auto result = con.context->Query(query, false);
+	REQUIRE(!result->HasError());
+	auto types = result->GetTypes();
+	auto names = IdentifiersToStrings(result->GetNames());
+	return make_uniq<ArrowTestFactory>(std::move(types), std::move(names), std::move(result), false, client_properties,
+	                                   *con.context);
+}
+
+// The sort operator the plan picked, so a failure names both plans rather than printing npos.
+static string PlanKind(const string &explain) {
+	if (explain.find("TOP_N") != string::npos) {
+		return "TOP_N";
+	}
+	if (explain.find("ORDER_BY") != string::npos) {
+		return "ORDER_BY";
+	}
+	return "NEITHER";
+}
+
+// The row estimate the plan gave the scan, as rendered by EXPLAIN.
+static string ScanEstimate(const string &explain, const string &scan) {
+	auto pos = explain.find(scan);
+	REQUIRE(pos != string::npos);
+	auto tilde = explain.find('~', pos);
+	REQUIRE(tilde != string::npos);
+	auto end = explain.find(" row", tilde);
+	REQUIRE(end != string::npos);
+	return explain.substr(tilde, end - tilde);
+}
+
+static string ExplainOf(shared_ptr<Relation> rel) {
+	auto explain_result = rel->Explain();
+	REQUIRE(!explain_result->HasError());
+	auto &mat = explain_result->Cast<MaterializedQueryResult>();
+	return mat.GetValue(1, 0).ToString();
+}
+
+TEST_CASE("Arrow scan: ORDER BY ... LIMIT plans a TOP_N like a native table", "[arrow]") {
+	DuckDB db;
+	Connection con(db);
+	// Large enough that LIMIT 10000 is a small fraction of the data, which is what decides the plan.
+	REQUIRE(!con.Query("CREATE TABLE src AS SELECT i AS price FROM range(2000000) tbl(i)")->HasError());
+	REQUIRE(!con.Query("SET profiling_renderer_settings = MAP {'operator_casing': 'upper'}")->HasError());
+
+	auto factory = MakeArrowFactory(con, "SELECT * FROM src");
+	const auto params = ArrowTestHelper::ConstructArrowScan(*factory);
+	auto arrow_explain = ExplainOf(con.TableFunction("arrow_scan", params)->Order("price DESC")->Limit(10000));
+	auto native_explain = ExplainOf(con.Table("src")->Order("price DESC")->Limit(10000));
+
+	// The same rows and the same query, so only the source differs.
+	INFO("arrow scan estimate: " << ScanEstimate(arrow_explain, "ARROW_SCAN")
+	                             << ", native estimate: " << ScanEstimate(native_explain, "SEQ_SCAN"));
+	REQUIRE(PlanKind(native_explain) == "TOP_N");
+	REQUIRE(PlanKind(arrow_explain) == "TOP_N");
+}

title: [Parser] Add `DialectExtension` extension API
body:
This PR is part of https://github.com/duckdblabs/duckdb-internal/issues/10434

And includes https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb/pull/25437

### `DialectExtension`
Interface exposing virtual methods:
- `ApplyGrammarChanges` - direct access to the `ParsedGrammar` to modify.
- `CreateKeywordHelper` - provide a custom `PEGKeywordHelper` implementation.
- `CreateTokenizer` - provide a custom `Tokenizer` implementation.
- `CreateMatcherFactory` - provide a custom `MatcherFactory` implementation.

The `DialectExtension` is named, registered in the `ExtensionCallbackManager`.
The available dialects can be listed by `FROM duckdb_dialects()`.
The `current_dialect` setting can be changed to one of these options to select a dialect.

When a `DialectExtension` is selected, its `CompiledGrammar` will be created and cached in the instance. Any `CompiledGrammar::Get(...)` calls afterwards will return the compiled grammar of the dialect, until the `current_dialect` is changed to another dialect or `RESET` to NULL.
The `DialectExtension` can also define a `DialectCompatibilityMode` to set the `dialect_compatibility_mode` setting when the dialect is selected, removing the need for manually changing the `dialect_compatibility_mode` setting.

Note that any `GrammarExtension` will be ignored by the system as long as a `DialectExtension` is active.

title: Fix checkpoint corrupting -0.0 into 0.0 for FLOAT/DOUBLE columns
body:
## Summary
`NumericStats::IsConstant()` treats `min == max` as proof a segment is constant, but `-0.0 == 0.0` for floats without being bit-identical. Checkpoint then collapses such segments to one value, losing the sign of zero. RLE has the same flaw: it merges adjacent values with `==`, folding a `-0.0` run into a `0.0` run.

## Fix
- `numeric_stats.cpp`: `IsConstant()` returns `false` for `FLOAT`/`DOUBLE` when min is zero.
- `rle.cpp`: added `RLEValueEqual<T>`, comparing bits instead of `==` for `float`/`double`.

## Tests
- `constant_negative_zero.test`: checks `signbit()` survives checkpoint/restart for both the constant-segment and forced-RLE paths.

Fixes #25580

title: fix(capi): handle dictionary columns across Arrow importer chunks
body:
Fixes #25611.

Dictionary-encoded Arrow columns imported through the v2 C API were incorrectly using the parent slice offset (`chunk_offset`) when rebuilding the dictionary in `ColumnArrowToDuckDBDictionary`. Because the v2 importer creates a fresh scan state per slice, the dictionary is rebuilt for every chunk — so slices with `chunk_offset > 0` read past the dictionary bounds, producing wrong values for every chunk after the first and risking out-of-bounds access (reported as a segfault at seven rows with a three-value dictionary and an import batch of two).

The fix reads the dictionary array from offset 0 while preserving the parent index offset for the actual row indices. The index array is still read at the parent `chunk_offset`; only the dictionary payload is rebuilt from the start.

Regression coverage added for:
- a dictionary smaller than the import batch,
- a dictionary larger than the import batch,
- a dictionary exactly matching the import batch size.

Validation (`build/reldebug/test/unittest`, RelWithDebInfo):
- `[capi_v2][arrow]` 18/18 passed (625 assertions)
- `[capi_v2]` 443 passed, 1 skipped
- `[capi][arrow]` 3/3 passed (10117 assertions)

title: ASOF JOIN returns a different payload row for the same query on static tables
body:
### What happens?

When build rows tie on the ASOF ordering key, the join takes whichever of them the sort left last, and the sort key holds only the partition and ordering columns, so nothing breaks the tie and the same query over unchanged tables gives different answers run to run. Setting `threads = 1` makes it stable.



### To Reproduce


```sql
CREATE TABLE b AS SELECT (i % 50)::INT k, ((i / 4)::INT % 1000) t, i::INT w FROM range(200000) s(i);
CREATE TABLE p AS SELECT (i % 50)::INT k, ((i * 7) % 1000)::INT t FROM range(5000) s(i);

SELECT sum(x.w) FROM p ASOF JOIN b x ON p.k = x.k AND p.t >= x.t;
SELECT sum(x.w) FROM p ASOF JOIN b x ON p.k = x.k AND p.t >= x.t;
SELECT sum(x.w) FROM p ASOF JOIN b x ON p.k = x.k AND p.t >= x.t;

SET threads = 1;
SELECT sum(x.w) FROM p ASOF JOIN b x ON p.k = x.k AND p.t >= x.t;
SELECT sum(x.w) FROM p ASOF JOIN b x ON p.k = x.k AND p.t >= x.t;
```

```
502097880
473037880
565717880
485497880
485497880
```

Three evaluations of one query in one process, tables untouched between them.

`sum(x.t)` over the same join is `2469400` every time, so the ordering column is stable and it is the payload chosen among ties that moves. Below `asof_loop_join_threshold` (default 64 probe rows) the plan is a nested loop join with an `arg_max` aggregate rather than `ASOF_JOIN`, and that path keeps the first tied row instead of the last: with `p(k,t) = (1,2)` and `b(k,t,w) = (1,1,1),(1,1,2),(1,1,3)` it returns `1`, and `SET asof_loop_join_threshold = 0` returns `3` on the same rows.

Either a documented tie-break or a stable one would be fine.

title: EXTERNAL RESOURCE: allow first class externally managed resources (SQL syntax on top of table functions)

labels.name: Needs Documentation
labels.description: Use for issues or PRs that require changes in the documentation

body:
Based on https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb/pull/23731 infrastructure, this PR adds SQL level interface for allowing interfacing with external resources as first class citizens of DuckDB SQL.

## 1. Syntax the parser now accepts

Durable — the resource outlives any one attachment, and only `DESTROY` will tear it down:
```sql
CREATE   EXTERNAL RESOURCE '<resource-type>' AS <name> [(RESOURCE_OPTS...)];
REGISTER EXTERNAL RESOURCE '<resource-type>' AS <name> FROM <handle>;
DESTROY  EXTERNAL RESOURCE <name>;
SHOW [ALL] EXTERNAL RESOURCES;
```

Scoped - the resource lives and dies with the attachment/connection:
```sql
ATTACH  TO NEW TEMPORARY EXTERNAL RESOURCE '<resource-type>' [(RESOURCE_OPTS...)] AS <db-name> [(ATTACH_OPTS...)];
CONNECT TO NEW TEMPORARY EXTERNAL RESOURCE '<resource-type>' [(RESOURCE_OPTS...)];

ATTACH  TO EXTERNAL RESOURCE <name> AS <db-name> [(ATTACH_OPTS...)];
CONNECT TO EXTERNAL RESOURCE <name> [(CONNECT_OPTS...)];
```

`NEW TEMPORARY` is the ownership marker: it provisions a fresh resource the statement OWNS and reaps on `DETACH`/`DISCONNECT`. Without it, `<name>` refers to an already-registered resource the statement only bottow — resources are managed explicitly and require a `DESTROY`.

## 2. Examples

### 2a. CONNECT TO NEW EXTERNAL RESOURCE — the resource lives and dies with the connection

```sql
LOAD aws;
CALL enable_logging('ExternalResource', storage='stdout');
CONNECT TO NEW EXTERNAL RESOURCE 'aws:cloudformation:quack-on-ec2' (REGION 'us-east-1');
DISCONNECT;
```
(logging to in-memory table / file might be preferable, consider https://duckdb.org/docs/lts/operations_manual/logging/overview)
Note this requires about 2 minutes to spin up an EC2 machine from a given public recipe that references a publicly available AMI, setup quack, obtain a SSL certificate, and some polling wait time. This can be significantly reduced by improving setup, but that's independent.

The log narrates the whole lifecycle — `CONNECT` provisions and polls until resource is ready, `DISCONNECT` reaps:

### 2c. Resources explicit lifetime: creation / adoption / borrow / destroy

An orphan is recoverable: `ADOPT` takes over its handle under a local name. Borrowing an existing
resource attaches to it without taking ownership.

```sql
SHOW ALL EXTERNAL RESOURCES;
SET VARIABLE handle_map = (SELECT handle FROM duckdb_external_resources(discover:=all) LIMIT 1);
--- syntax here to be improved, but `handle_map` is the representation of the resource

ADOPT EXTERNAL RESOURCE 'aws:cloudformation:quack-on-ec2' AS resource FROM getvariable('handle_map');
--- name a resource for local usage

ATTACH TO EXTERNAL RESOURCE resource AS quack_server;
-- borrows: no deleter bound, quack_server will be of the type dictated by the resource, in this case `quack`
CREATE TABLE quack_server.T AS FROM range(42);

CONNECT quack_server;
.tables 
--- table T should show
DISCONNECT;

DETACH quack_server;
--- ATTACH was not tied to lifetime of resource, so no tear down 
SHOW ALL EXTERNAL RESOURCES;
--- all resources, as above or possibly more

DESTROY EXTERNAL RESOURCE resource;
--- explicit DESTROY will tear down the resource
SHOW ALL EXTERNAL RESOURCES;
```

## 3. Ownership and the registry

The lifetime story is one invariant: the statement that provisions a resource is the one that reaps it. `NEW` binds a deleter onto the `AttachedDatabase`, and `DETACH`/`DISCONNECT` runs it. A borrowed resource binds no deleter, so detaching leaves it registered for a later `DESTROY`.

`CREATE`/`ADOPT` register an instance in an instance-scoped manager; `DESTROY` tears down and deregisters; `SHOW ALL EXTERNAL RESOURCES` / `duckdb_external_resources()` lists them unioning in resources discovered via each type's `list` callback - the reconciliation view that feeds `ADOPT`, so a resource that outlived its DuckDB process can be recovered rather than orphaned.

> Delete (that might trigger remote operations) will NOT be guaranteed to be always run. Recomendation is any/all of the following:
* have some form of idle or timeout based automatic close of the resource provider side
* have a mean of listing such resources (it's an opt-in capability of `external_resource_types`)
* native observability (e.g. `aws'`s cloudformation API)

Not load bearing, but pleasant for debugging, testing and explaining the mechanism, is a new logging type `ExternalResources`, that would allow after (for example) `CALL enable_logging('ExternalResources', storage=stdout)` to demonstrate progress.

Currently this works and has been designed for using `aws:cloudformation` tagged stacks to store state and making it work with the default provided template, but cloudformation templates are pluggable, allowing reuse and adaptation.
There is further work on improving the template AND generalizing to other templates, but this is oversized enough to be worth as is.

Thanks to many discussions that refined this idea, and to @samansmink in particular for the clean idea of the `WITH EXTERNAL RESOURCE`.

body:
(Part 4 https://github.com/duckdblabs/duckdb-internal/issues/10748 is for porting everything related to insertion in the ART, there will be several PRs, hence 4a).

The big change here is PrefixHandle::Split, it is mostly the same with one difference: we allocate the replacement node (node being inserted at the split point) before calling Split(), and now let Split() install it + handle gate status installation internally. This simplified the code somewhat with PrefixHandles. I walked through all possible permutations of the logic; note that afterwards, the caller still installs the returned value in the replacement node at the split byte. 

### Prefix split cases examples

`[]` = prefix bytes, `R` = replacement Node4, `*` = gate (note that * means the pointer to the object has the gate set, not the node itself), `T` = unchanged subtree. Prefix capacity is 4 for illustration.

```text

CASE                 BEFORE                   AFTER SPLIT                          AFTER CALLER ATTACHES CHILD

Middle byte (b)       [abcd] -> T              Tree:   [a] -> R                     [a] -> R --b--> [cd] -> T
                                              Return: [cd] -> T

First byte (a)        [abc] -> T               Tree:   R                            R --a--> [bc] -> T
                                              Return: [bc] -> T
                                              Original prefix freed.

Last, partial (c)    [abc] -> T               Tree:   [ab] -> R                    [ab] -> R --c--> T
                                              Return: T
                                              No suffix allocated.

Last, full (d)       [abcd] -> T              Tree:   [abc] -> R                   [abc] -> R --d--> T
                                              Return: T
                                              No suffix allocated.

Only byte (a)        [a] -> T                 Tree:   R                            R --a--> T
                                              Return: T
                                              Original freed; no suffix.


GATED ORIGINAL PREFIX — these prefix bytes belong to the row-ID key

First byte (a)       *[abc] -> T              Tree:   *R                           *R --a--> [bc] -> T
                                              Return: [bc] -> T
                                              Original freed; gate transferred.

Middle byte (b)      *[abc] -> T              Tree:   *[a] -> R                    *[a] -> R --b--> [c] -> T
                                              Return: [c] -> T
                                              Gate stays on original pointer.

Last, partial (c)    *[abc] -> T              Tree:   *[ab] -> R                   *[ab] -> R --c--> T
                                              Return: T
                                              Gate stays; no suffix.

Last, full (d)       *[abcd] -> T             Tree:   *[abc] -> R                  *[abc] -> R --d--> T
                                              Return: T
                                              Gate stays; no suffix.

Only byte (a)        *[a] -> T                Tree:   *R                           *R --a--> T
                                              Return: T
                                              Original freed; gate transferred.


SUFFIX CONTINUATION

Ordinary, at b       [abcd] -> [efgh] -> T    Tree:   [a] -> R                     [a] -> R --b--> [cdef] -> [gh] -> T
                                              Return: [cdef] -> [gh] -> T
                                              Old [efgh] allocation freed.

Gated, at b          [abcd] -> *[xy] -> T     Tree:   [a] -> R                     [a] -> R --b--> [cd] -> *[xy] -> T
                                              Return: [cd] -> *[xy] -> T
                                              Gated node preserved.
```
