title: ConstantOrderNormalizationRule reorders integer chains without a range check

labels.name: PR submitted
labels.description: A pull request was submitted to fix the issue

body:
### What happens?

`ConstantOrderNormalizationRule` hoists the foldable leaves of a commutative integer chain to the front with no range check, so the chain is evaluated in an order the query did not write and an addition that fits raises an overflow error. It flips back under `disabled_optimizers = 'expression_rewriter'`.



### To Reproduce

```sql
CREATE TABLE t(a INTEGER, b INTEGER);
INSERT INTO t VALUES (2147483645, -2);

SET disabled_optimizers = 'expression_rewriter';
SELECT (a + 1) + (b + 2) FROM t;

SET disabled_optimizers = '';
SELECT (a + 1) + (b + 2) FROM t;
```

```
2147483646
Out of Range Error: Overflow in addition of INT32 (3 + 2147483645)!
```

PostgreSQL 17.11 gives `2147483646` and its plan keeps the written order.

With `explain_output = 'OPTIMIZED_ONLY'` the projection is `((3 + a) + b)`: the rule flattens the chain and moves the foldable leaves to the front, `ConstantFoldingRule` folds `1 + 2` into `3`, and `3 + a` is evaluated first, which overflows where the written order does not. The rule is registered at `src/optimizer/optimizer.cpp:50` and `ConstantFoldingRule` at `:51`.

title: Add IMMEDIATE and DEFERRED constraint timing syntax
body:
```sql
statement error
CREATE TABLE deferred_column_unique(i INTEGER UNIQUE DEFERRED);
----
Not implemented Error: Deferred UNIQUE constraints are not implemented yet

statement error
CREATE TABLE deferred_column_primary_key(i INTEGER PRIMARY KEY DEFERRED);
----
Not implemented Error: Deferred PRIMARY KEY constraints are not implemented yet
```

Add IMMEDIATE and DEFERRED to the grammar for UNIQUE and PRIMARY KEY constraints. DEFERRED throws not implemented for now; IMMEDIATE keeps the current behavior. Part 1 of implementing https://github.com/duckdblabs/duckdb-internal/issues/6885, subsequent PR will be the actual implementation for UNIQUE + PRIMARY keys.

Internally we keep three values: DEFAULT, IMMEDIATE, and DEFERRED. DEFAULT means no modifier was specified, and currently behaves the same as IMMEDIATE. We preserve the distinction so that we can change the default in the future without changing constraints that were explicitly declared IMMEDIATE. The declared mode is preserved when copying, rendering back to SQL, and serializing constraints.

For persistent tables, explicit IMMEDIATE requires storage version v2.0.0 or newer, since older formats cannot preserve the declared mode. We reject this up front rather than silently turn IMMEDIATE into DEFAULT when reopening the database. Existing older files can still be opened, and constraints without an explicit modifier continue to work with older storage versions. Temporary and in-memory tables do not have this storage restriction. DEFERRED still throws not implemented regardless of storage version.

Note: also fixes a regression in the parser that was allowing various ADD COLUMN <constraint>'s to parse, even though those constraints were not actually implemented and were silently ignored. Added parser errors for those, as well as a test for each one (each test case can be updated as that constraint is actually implemented for ADD COLUMN). I will backport this specific fix to 2.0 as well.

--------------------------------------

Note in the issue it was proposed to make DEFERRED the default (right now we have IMMEDIATE behavior by default). I think it makes sense to start out implementing DEFERRED as an opt-in at first, and after it is fully supported we can consider making it the default, perhaps in v3.0.

There are a lot of considerations here, but I think taken together they come down to allowing us to implement full DEFERRED support in a piece-meal manner before deciding on making the switch to having it be the default:

1) It changes existing semantics for test cases + code running transactions in a big way, since we would allow an inconsistent state w.r.t. constraints during transaction processing. This can be useful, but other databases such as Postgres also have deferred checking as an "opt-in" feature, not the default mode of processing. So this could potentially be confusing for people used to eager constraint checking semantics as a default.

2) We can implement the full DEFERRED feature set piece-meal, i.e. the subsequent PR will just start out implementing it for UNIQUE + PRIMARY KEYs, then we can do FKs, etc.

3) We keep the grammar simple at first: a constraint can explicitly specify IMMEDIATE or DEFERRED, or leave the modifier out to use the default. There are also some considerations around "toggling" of modes. There is some not so friendly looking SQL in the standard for setting things like DEFERRABLE INITIALLY DEFERRED, SET CONSTRAINTS, etc. This looks like a good opportunity for some more friendly SQL, but supporting toggling and figuring out a nicer grammar can be a future PR. This PR just records the declared mode; it does not add toggling.

4) Keep ON CONFLICT the same for now under IMMEDIATE behavior, and when we implement DEFERRED I think we can initially just reject using DEFERRED constraints as an arbiter.

This PR adds a first iteration of support for the glorious `MATCH_RECOGNIZE`, a way of doing pattern matching in SQL.

```SQL
FROM ticks MATCH_RECOGNIZE(
    PARTITION BY symbol ORDER BY ts
    MEASURES FIRST(ts) AS started, count(*) AS len
    ONE ROW PER MATCH AFTER MATCH SKIP PAST LAST ROW
    PATTERN (onset dip+ climb+)
    DEFINE dip AS dip.price < PREV(dip.price),
           climb AS climb.price > PREV(climb.price))
```

Internally, this is implemented by converting the regex-like pattern into a small program of match, split, and jump instructions that is traversed depth-first.

title: Add sql tokenizer to C API
body:
This exposes the sql tokenizer through the new C API. There's not much interesting happening I think:
- We add a `tokenize_sql(conn, sql, *out_iterator, *err)` function that takes a `duckdb_v2_str sql` string and creates an opaque `token_iterator`. Users can call `token_iterator_next(*out_type, *out_start, *out_length, *err)` to get the token type (from the `TOKEN_TYPE` enum), the start position in the input string, and the length of the lexeme in the input string.
- The C++ API wraps this by adding the `Connection::Tokenize(sql)` method, which returns a vector of `Token`s (a struct that includes the type, start index and length)

The reason that the tokenization happens in the context of a connection is to respect any grammar extensions that might be loaded on that connection. The tokenizer is eager though, so the iterator does not need the connection after its been created.

title: Optimize keyword matching for the PEG parser
body:
This PR adds two optimizations for keyword matching: 
1. Each literal in the grammar gets an integer ID. We store both the keyword category using a `uint8_t` bitmask (a keyword may be in two categories) and a dense ID (`uint16_t`) which we cache on the first lookup. This avoids repeated string comparisons and keyword-category lookups. 
2. For rules consisting only of literals, such as `UnreservedKeyword` we create a special `LiteralChoiceMatcher`. It uses the token's ID to directly select the matching branch, avoid attempts that would fail anyway. We do still go to the respective KeywordMatcher to update token position and return a ParseResult. 

Grammar extensions and custom matchers should not be influenced. 

Benchmarks show a 24-34% improvement for TPC-H, TPC-DS, Flummi, and AoC. Perhaps I should create some parser specific performance tests.

body:
https://github.com/duckdblabs/duckdb-internal/issues/9231 

WIP, just a draft to see if this is worth introducing as an API (since the API was requested, we are trying to find a use for a batch key preparation API in core). The gains were very small here, although there were no regressions and it could indeed help in some scenarios with IN/equality filters, and of course when batching together more keys. 

Batch equality lookups in ART index scans, including `IN` filters and equality filters pushed down from joins.

Previously, each extracted lookup value was converted into a separate equality expression and scan state. The new path stores multiple equality values in one scan state, generates ART keys in chunks, and acquires the ART lock once per chunk. Index traversal still happens once per key though.

Measured on an Apple M1 Pro (8 CPU cores, 16 GiB RAM) with 4 threads.

Each type uses a 100-million-row table, a unique ART index, and a BIGINT payload. Keys are distributed across physical storage. Queries compute `count(*)` and `sum(payload)` over rows selected by an IN filter, join, or range predicate.

I also ran this on a pretty large table to showcase a scenario where we couldn't just do a regular table scan to beat the index.

title: Allow Pinning/Unpinning of ColumnReader::block
body:
`ColumnReader::block`, the buffer holding each page's decompressed data, was previously allocated with an `Allocator` and was always kept pinned.

This moves `block` onto the buffer manager (`BlockHandle`/`BufferHandle`), pinning it only around each vector's read and unpinning it in between. `ByteBuffer` was changed to use an offset-based cursor instead of an absolute pointer. Further, every decoder that caches a pointer into `block` (dictionary, RLE, delta-binary-packed, byte-stream-split) now rebases itself against the new address after each re-pin.

One buffer was deliberately left on `Allocator`: the bloom filter built while writing a dictionary page. It's short-lived and never re-pinned, so buffer-manager tracking would only add overhead there with no eviction benefit.

I ran a small benchmark locally, no speed regression, and it now keeps working once memory gets tight enough that main just runs out of memory.

Also includes a small unrelated build fix in `expression_binder.cpp` I hit along the way.

This looks like a lot of changes, but a lot of the changes are because many of the functions were renamed for formatting reasons (ie. `inc()` -> `Inc()`).

This also happens without any `SET`, because the setting defaults to the `HTTP_PROXY` env var. So on a machine where `HTTP_PROXY=https://...`, every `INSTALL` and every httpfs read/write fails out of the box. The only way around it is `SET http_proxy = ''` and losing the proxy.

Just stripping the `https://` prefix wouldn't fix it either since the proxy expects TLS, and DuckDB always talks plaintext to the proxy, so it then fails with a connection error instead (see repro 3). I understand that `libcurl` can do TLS to a proxy.

### To Reproduce

1. Minimal repro in the CLI:
```
SET http_proxy = 'https://proxy.example.com:3128';
INSTALL some_extension;
```
Expect to see the error:
```
Invalid Input Error:
Failed to parse http_proxy 'https://proxy.example.com:3128' into a host and port
```

2. From the environment without `SET`:
```
HTTP_PROXY=https://proxy.example.com:3128 duckdb -c "SELECT current_setting('http_proxy');"
HTTP_PROXY=https://proxy.example.com:3128 duckdb -c "INSTALL some_extension;"
```
Expect:
```
https://proxy.example.com:3128
Invalid Input Error: Failed to parse http_proxy 'https://proxy.example.com:3128' into a host and port
```

3. Pointing DuckDB at the TLS port as plain host:port:
```
INSTALL httpfs; LOAD httpfs;
SET http_proxy = 'localhost:3129';
SELECT size FROM read_blob('https://storage.googleapis.com/sdsc_demo25/duckdb_test/ne_10m_airports.zip');
```
```
-- httpfs_client_implementation = 'curl'
IO Error: Failure when receiving data from the peer error for HTTP HEAD to 'https://storage.googleapis.com/...'
-- httpfs_client_implementation = 'httplib'
IO Error: Failed to read connection error for HTTP HEAD to 'https://storage.googleapis.com/...'
```

Related: https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb/issues/6064

I am happy to fix this and can open the PRs if this approach is alright:
- `duckdb`: accept `https://` in `ParseHTTPProxyHost`, add an `http_proxy_use_ssl` flag to `HTTPParams` (default port 443 for https)
- `httpfs` (curl client): pass `https://host:port` to `CURLOPT_PROXY` when the flag is set
- httplib clients (core install path and the httpfs httplib backend): throw a clear error pointing at `httpfs_client_implementation = 'curl'` rather than talking plaintext to a TLS port

title: Join-order plan reconstruction (GenerateJoins) fires INTERNAL errors: "Cost predicate consumed before operator occurrence" and "Operator occurrence reconstructed more than once"
body:
### What happens?

`QueryGraphManager::GenerateJoins` in `src/optimizer/join_order/query_graph_manager.cpp` rebuilds the plan chosen by the join-order dynamic program back into a logical operator tree. During that walk it enforces two invariants on the plan it was handed, and both can be violated, each surfacing as an `InternalException`:

- `src/optimizer/join_order/query_graph_manager.cpp:624` — `reconstructed_operators.insert(descriptor->index)` fails, so the same operator occurrence is reconstructed twice:
  ```
  INTERNAL Error: Operator occurrence %llu was reconstructed more than once
  ```
- `src/optimizer/join_order/query_graph_manager.cpp:630` — an operator's `costing_predicate_indices` points at a filter whose `filter` is already null, i.e. a cost predicate was consumed by an earlier operator occurrence:
  ```
  INTERNAL Error: Cost predicate %llu was consumed before operator occurrence %llu
  ```

Both are consistency assertions on the reconstruction, so reaching either means the dynamic program produced a plan in which an operator occurrence (or its costing predicate) is assigned inconsistently — the same occurrence reachable from two positions in the rebuilt join tree, or a predicate owned by two occurrences. They are not user errors; the query is well-formed and the plan should reconstruct cleanly. The neighbouring throws in the same function (lines 191, 472, 481, 620, 646) guard the same reconstruction, which is why a single ill-formed plan can trip whichever check it reaches first.

Both are reached by queries that join windowed sub-queries under a mix of join types. The estimate drives the plan, so the failure depends on table statistics: stripping columns or rows changes the cardinality estimate, the plan changes, and the assertion no longer fires. The full standard schema is therefore kept in the reproduction below.

### To Reproduce

title: Vuln184: Integer Truncation in `ArgMinMaxValueAssign::Assign` Leads to Heap Buffer Overflow with Large Strings

body:
### What happens?

In `extension/core_functions/aggregate/distributive/arg_min_max.cpp`, `ArgMinMaxValueAssign<string_t>::Assign()` computes the arena allocation size by calling `UnsafeNumericCast<uint32_t>(NextPowerOfTwo(len))` where `len` is the byte length of the argument string. For any argument string whose length is in the range `(2^31, 2^32-1]`, `NextPowerOfTwo` returns `2^32`, and the subsequent `uint32_t` cast truncates it to `0`. In a release build, `ArenaAllocator::Allocate(0)` returns a zero-length region, and the immediately following `memcpy(ptr, new_value.GetData(), len)` writes gigabytes past that region, producing a heap buffer overflow. The bug is reachable by either the `arg_min()` or `arg_max()` aggregate when the first (argument) column is a VARCHAR/BLOB.

### To Reproduce


```sql
SET threads=1;
SELECT arg_min(s, 1)
FROM (
    SELECT string_agg(repeat('A', 100000000), '') AS s
    FROM range(22)
) t;
```

title: Bind planner and executor builtins through the catalog
body:
#25472 moved the optimizer rewrites onto the catalog, so a builtin they introduce keeps the catalog and schema name its entry stamped on it. While writing that PR I kept finding the same factory-and-bind shape outside `src/optimizer`, and this picks those up.

Decorrelation is the clearest case. `FlattenDependentJoins` builds the `ROW_NUMBER()` it pushes onto the LHS with `RowNumberFun::GetFunction().Bind(...)`, and so do the full-outer-join pairing path, `WITH ORDINALITY`, set operations and the asof join. `plan_subquery` does the same for the `min`/`max`, `count`, `count_star` and `first` it introduces while flattening subqueries, the delim-join hash table does it for its correlated counts, and `bind_unnest_expression` builds `struct_extract` that way — the `StructExtractFun::GetFunction().Bind(...)` Maxxen pointed at in the review on #25260 that started all of this. Around twenty-five sites in total.

Window functions had no lookup helper yet, but they needed nothing new: `WindowFunctionCatalogEntry` stamps catalog and schema onto its overloads exactly like the scalar and aggregate entries, `WindowFunctionSet::GetFunctionByArguments` already exists, and `WindowFunction::Bind` mirrors `ScalarFunction::Bind`. So `GetBuiltinWindowFunction` is a direct transcription of the aggregate one. I also moved `builtin_function_lookup` from `duckdb/optimizer` to `duckdb/function`, because multi-file column mapping needs it and having `src/common` include an optimizer header inverts the layering.

Converting the call sites turned out not to be enough for the aggregates, which is the more interesting half of this. After the conversion I checked what the bound functions actually carried and they were still unqualified. The reason is `BoundAggregateFunction::ReplaceImplementation`: it copies `name`, `schema_name` and `catalog_name` off the replacement, and every caller passes a function built by a factory rather than one handed out by a catalog entry. `BindFirst` reaches its type-specialized implementation through it, so does the `sum` to `sum_no_overflow` swap in statistics propagation, and so do `quantile`, `mode`, `histogram` and `arg_min`/`arg_max` on decimals. The qualification the entry had just set was being dropped a moment later. That also means this was never only a planner problem: `SELECT sum(v) FROM t` loses it too, however the aggregate was bound.

The replacement is a specialized implementation of the function we were bound from, not a different function, so it should not be the authority on where that function came from. I made `ReplaceImplementation` take the replacement's qualification only when it actually has one. The name stays assignable, deliberately: `CountPropagateStats` renames `count` to `count_star` through this path when the child cannot be null, and the collated min/max path really does hand over a catalog-derived `arg_min`/`arg_max`, which carries its own qualification and should win.

A few things worth flagging. `first` and `last` looked like the risky conversion, since the call sites ask for `FirstFunctionGetter::GetFunction(type)` and the catalog set holds only an `ANY` and a `DECIMAL` entry. They resolve to the same thing: `BindFirst` specializes the implementation for the argument type and applies the same direct-rewrite, single-value-identity and statistics callbacks the factory sets directly, plus `SetDistinctDependent`, which the factory path never set. In `AddCorrelatedFirstAggregates` I replaced a hand-built `BoundAggregateExpression` carrying null bind data with a real bind, so code now runs there that previously did not — the end state is the same, but it is a deliberate behavioural change rather than a mechanical substitution.

I left `src/planner/filter` alone on purpose, and added a comment saying why. The bloom, prefix-range, dynamic and optional filter functions are registered, but only so that plans containing them can be serialized and deserialized: `TableFilterFunctions::Bind` throws "Table filter functions are for internal use only!", and the call sites build the expression directly with hand-made bind data. Routing them through the catalog would turn every dynamic filter into a binder error. This is the same situation as the compressed materialization helpers, which #25472 left for the same reason. Cast functions remain unqualified too, since they come from the cast function set rather than a catalog entry, and that is a separate piece of work.

The test from #25472 grew a branch for window expressions, which hold either an aggregate or a window function depending on whether you wrote `sum(x) OVER ()` or `row_number()`, so the planner-introduced ones are visible to it at all.

title: convert recursion to stack-based transversal of variant to parquet
body:
Closes https://github.com/duckdblabs/duckdb-internal/issues/10306

Fix unbounded recursion when converting deeply nested VARIANT arrays and objects to Parquet.

`EmitIterator` previously used recursion to transverse nested VARIANT values. A deeply nested VARIANT could exhaust the native stack and cause a stack overflow.

### Changes

* Replace recursive traversal in `EmitIterator` with stack-based traversal.
* Track the current container and child index in each frame, allowing deeply nested values to be processed without growing the native call stack.
* Add a maximum VARIANT nesting depth of 16, following the pattern of `Geometry` (JSON), so that very deep values are not processed.
* Collapse `BeginArray` and `BeginObject` into `BeginContainer`.
* Reserve the stack up front using the nesting limit to avoid reallocations during traversal.

### Testing

Added regression coverage for VARIANT arrays at the maximum nesting depth and beyond it.
* Verified 16 levels are successfully converted.
* Verified 17 and 18 levels fail with the expected nesting-depth error.
* Reproduced the original deeply nested (~15,000 levels) input and confirmed it now returns a controlled `InvalidInputException` instead of causing a stack overflow/crash.

title: Experiment: Flatten ParserResult and MatchStack
body:
Follow up of [PR](https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb/pull/25520). This PR also flattens the `ParseResult`. See [flattening](https://www.cs.cornell.edu/~asampson/blog/flattening.html).

- Replaced individually allocated `ParseResult` objects with a contiguous slot pool.
- Added stable 32-bit `ParseResultRef` identifiers, so references remain valid when the pool grows.
- Stored list and repeat children in a shared packed child-reference pool.
- Changed matcher results and packrat entries to carry IDs instead of pointers.
- Changed transformer stack frames and inputs to carry IDs, resolving objects only when accessed.
- Preserved the existing typed transformer interface for `ListParseResult`, `OptionalParseResult`, and other result types.
- Restricted pooled allocation to the built-in `ParseResult` types at compile time.

Removes one heap allocation per `ParseResult` and reduces pointer chasing.
Preserves `ParseResult` lifetimes across matcher arena resets.

body:
Fixes #25532.

title: Fix integer truncation in ArgMinMaxValueAssign::Assign
body:
## Summary
`ArgMinMaxValueAssign<string_t>::Assign()` computed the arena allocation size via `UnsafeNumericCast<uint32_t>(NextPowerOfTwo(len))`. For a string length in `(2^31, 2^32-1]`, this returns `2^32`, which truncates to `0`, causing a zero-size allocation followed by a heap-overflowing `memcpy`.

## Fix
Widened `alloc_size` from `uint32_t` to `idx_t` in `arg_min_max.cpp`, dropping the truncating cast.

## Tests
- `arg_min_max_string_truncation_overflow.test_slow`: reproduces the truncation under a `memory_limit` too small to satisfy the correct allocation, so it deterministically fails cleanly (fixed) or crashes (unfixed).

Fixes #25577

title: Fix ORDER BY turning -0.0 into 0.0 for FLOAT/DOUBLE columns
body:
## Summary
Root cause: `Sort::Sort` reconstructs any output column that's also an `ORDER BY` key by decoding it back from the internal sort key rather than keeping a separate payload copy. The sort key encoding for `FLOAT`/`DOUBLE` (`Radix::EncodeFloat`/`EncodeDouble`) intentionally maps `-0.0` and `0.0` to the same bit pattern so they compare equal, but that makes the encoding non-injective, and decoding it back always yields `+0.0`.

## Fix
 In `src/common/sort/sort.cpp`, when a key column's type contains `FLOAT`/`DOUBLE`, route it through the payload instead of aliasing it to the decoded sort key, so the original bits (including signed zero) are preserved.


## Tests
- Added `test/sql/order/order_by_negative_zero.test` covering `signbit()` and `1.0/v` before/after sorting on `DOUBLE` and `FLOAT`, plus the materialized-CTE case from the issue report.

Fixes #25417

title: Fix rolled-back DELETE poisoning uncheckpointed_delete_commit
body:
TLDR: In the current implementation, whenever we have a rollback-ed deletion operation, row group checkpoint cannot enter into fast path.

Background introduction
- `uncheckpointed_delete_commit` is used to decide whether the current row group has uncommitted delete operations, and could be used to [reuse metadata](https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb/blob/0691eeb9d699640f272ab4e52a7aaf2ec8afe85c/src/storage/table/row_group.cpp#L1615) on checkpoint
- Checkpoint reusing metadata is the fast path and is extremely beneficial to write performance, for example, it contains segment stats (i.e., min/max/count) and compression method, etc, so we don't need to re-calculate

In the current implementation, 
- Deletion rollback is implemented as record deletion commit id as [`NOT_DELETE_ID`](https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb/blob/0691eeb9d699640f272ab4e52a7aaf2ec8afe85c/src/transaction/rollback_state.cpp#L37-L42), and [updates the `uncheckpointed_delete_commit`](https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb/blob/0691eeb9d699640f272ab4e52a7aaf2ec8afe85c/src/storage/table/row_version_manager.cpp#L202-L204) regardless
- Later on, even if we perform a checkpoint operation, the `uncheckpointed_delete_commit` won't be reset because `NOT_DELETE_ID` is the [largest integer](https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb/blob/0691eeb9d699640f272ab4e52a7aaf2ec8afe85c/src/common/constants.cpp#L22) and [visibility bound, as a normal transaction id, won't be able to reset](https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb/blob/0691eeb9d699640f272ab4e52a7aaf2ec8afe85c/src/storage/table/row_version_manager.cpp#L277-L281)
- Conclusion: all later checkpoints won't be able to enter into the fast path

In this PR, I propose a small code change, `NOT_DELETE_ID` is a well-known constant to represent unreachable deletion commit id, we special handle it and skip updating `uncheckpointed_delete_commit`.
